title: Transistors as switches
goals: Say how an NPN transistor switches a load to 0 V, and a PNP one switches it to the supply
Work out the base current and base resistor that drive a transistor fully on
Work out the heat in a transistor or MOSFET switch
Say when to use a MOSFET instead, and what its gate needs
Relate NPN and PNP to sinking and sourcing PLC inputs and outputs
summary:
A transistor used as a **switch** is either fully **off** (cut-off) or fully **on** (saturated), never in between.

**NPN** (bipolar junction transistor, BJT): the load goes between the supply and the **collector**; the **emitter** goes to 0 V. A small current into the **base** (with the base about **0.7 V** above the emitter) lets a much bigger current flow collector to emitter. It switches the load's 0 V side: a **low-side** switch, which **sinks** current.

**PNP**: the mirror image. Emitter to the supply, load from collector to 0 V; base pulled **below** the emitter to turn it on. A **high-side** switch, which **sources** current: the same as a PNP sensor or a PLC's sourcing output.

Current gain $h_{FE}$: $I_C \approx h_{FE} \times I_B$ when not saturated. To be sure it **saturates**, give it more base current than the bare minimum: $I_B = \frac{I_C}{h_{FE}} \times$ an overdrive of 2 to 5, using the datasheet's **minimum** $h_{FE}$.

Base resistor: $R_B = \frac{V_{in} - 0.7}{I_B}$.

Fully on, a BJT drops about 0.2 V ($V_{CE(sat)}$), so it wastes $P = V_{CE(sat)} \times I_C$.

A **MOSFET** is driven by **voltage** on its gate, not current: once the gate is high enough it acts as a small resistance, $R_{DS(on)}$, wasting $P = I^2 R_{DS(on)}$. Use a **logic-level** MOSFET from a 3.3 or 5 V output, a small gate resistor, and a pull-down so it stays off when the driver is not driving.

Switching a coil (relay, solenoid, contactor)? Fit a **flyback diode** across it.

resources.title: The Transistor as a Switch: A Practical Guide for Beginners

sources: Horowitz, P. and Hill, W.: The Art of Electronics, 3rd edition (Cambridge University Press), chapters 2 and 3
Kuphaldt, T. R.: Lessons in Electric Circuits, Volume III: Semiconductors (bipolar junction transistors; the transistor as a switch)
Onsemi: 2N2222A / BC337 and BS170 datasheets (typical small-signal transistor and MOSFET figures)

formulas.name: Collector current from base current
formulas.says: Below saturation, the collector current is the base current times the transistor's current gain.
symbols: the current gain (a number, from the datasheet)
formulas.example: 2 mA of base drive with a gain of 100: up to 200 mA.

formulas.name: Base resistor
formulas.says: The resistor takes the drive voltage less the base-emitter drop, at the base current you want.
symbols: the voltage that drives the base (V)

formulas.name: Heat in a saturated BJT
formulas.says: Fully on, the transistor still drops a little voltage, and that times the current becomes heat.
symbols: the collector-emitter voltage when saturated (about 0.2 V)

formulas.name: Heat in a MOSFET switch
formulas.says: A fully-on MOSFET behaves like a small resistor: its heat goes with the current squared.

bench.task: On a breadboard at 12 V DC, switch a 12 V relay coil (or a 12 V lamp under 200 mA) with an NPN transistor such as a BC337, driven from a 5 V supply through the base resistor you work out. Low voltage only.
check: Work out $R_B$ for twice the minimum base current (BC337: minimum gain about 100)
Fit a flyback diode across the relay coil, band to +12 V
Measure $V_{CE}$ with the transistor on: about 0.1–0.3 V means saturated
Halve the base drive (double $R_B$) and measure again: is it still saturated?

cards.q: An NPN transistor has a relay coil between +24 V and its collector; its emitter is at 0 V. What turns the relay on?
options: A small current into the base
Putting 24 V on the collector
Pulling the base below 0 V
Nothing: it is always on
cards.why: A small base current (base about 0.7 V above the emitter) lets a much larger current flow from collector to emitter, through the coil. No base current, no collector current: the relay is off.

cards.title: The NPN switch
cards.body:
An **NPN** transistor has three legs: **collector**, **base**, **emitter**.

As a switch: emitter to **0 V**, the load between the **supply** and the **collector**. Feed a small current into the **base** (the base sits about **0.7 V** above the emitter) and a much larger current flows from collector to emitter, through the load.

No base current: **off**. Plenty of base current: fully **on** (saturated), with only about **0.2 V** across it.

It switches the 0 V side of the load: a **low-side** switch that **sinks** current.
cards.more:
Think of a tap where a small push on a lever controls a big flow. The base current is the push; the collector current is the flow.

The base-emitter junction is a diode, so it needs about 0.7 V before base current flows, just as any silicon diode does.

In a switch, you want it either off or slammed fully on. In between (the 'active' region) it would have a few volts across it while carrying the full current, and get hot. Saturated, it has 0.1–0.3 V across it and stays cool.

An NPN sensor output and a PLC's sinking output are this circuit: the transistor connects the load's bottom end to 0 V.

cards.q: In an NPN low-side switch, which side of the load does the transistor connect?
options: The 0 V side
The supply side
Both sides at once
Neither: it is in parallel with the load
cards.why: The load goes from the supply to the collector, and the emitter is at 0 V: the transistor completes the load's path to 0 V. That is sinking.

cards.title: Gain, and driving it hard enough
cards.body:
The **current gain** $h_{FE}$ (often 50 to 300) says how much collector current a base current allows:

$$I_C = h_{FE} I_B$$

To **saturate** it for a load current $I_C$, the base needs at least $\frac{I_C}{h_{FE}}$. Gain varies a lot between parts and with temperature, so:

- use the datasheet's **minimum** $h_{FE}$
- give **2 to 5 times** that base current (overdrive)

Too little base drive and it sits half-on, with volts across it, and gets hot.
cards.more:
Numbers: a 200 mA relay coil and a transistor whose gain is at least 100. The base needs at least $200 \div 100 = 2$ mA. With an overdrive of 2.5: 5 mA.

Why not just 2 mA? The gain on the datasheet is a range: 100 to 300, say. A transistor at the bottom of that range, on a cold morning, with 2 mA in, is only just saturated. Give it 5 mA and every transistor of that type will saturate.

The price is a bit more current from whatever drives the base, which must be able to give it: a microcontroller pin is often limited to about 20 mA.

cards.q: A transistor must carry {ic} mA. Its minimum gain is {h}. What base current does it need, with an overdrive of {od}?
cards.why: Minimum base current is the collector current over the minimum gain; the overdrive makes sure every part saturates.

cards.title: The base resistor
cards.body:
The base is a diode to the emitter: it would take as much current as the driver could give. A **base resistor** sets the current:

$$R_B = \frac{V_{in} - 0.7}{I_B}$$

$V_{in}$ is the driving voltage (a PLC or microcontroller output), 0.7 V the base-emitter drop, $I_B$ the base current you want. Pick the nearest standard value **below** it, so the current comes out a little more, not less.
cards.more:
The resistor and the base-emitter junction share the drive voltage, like a resistor and an LED. The junction takes 0.7 V; the resistor takes the rest.

Numbers: a 5 V output wants to give 5 mA. $5 - 0.7 = 4.3$ V across the resistor; $4.3 \div 0.005 = 860$ Ω. Standard values near it: 820 Ω and 910 Ω. 820 gives $4.3 \div 820 = 5.2$ mA: good.

From a 24 V PLC output for the same 5 mA: $23.3 \div 0.005 = 4660$ Ω, so 4.7 kΩ gives 4.96 mA: just under, but with an overdrive already built in, fine, or use 3.9 kΩ.

Forget the resistor and the driver's output or the transistor dies.

cards.q: A {vin} V output drives a transistor's base. The base needs {ib} mA, and the base-emitter junction drops 0.7 V. What base resistor?
cards.why: The resistor takes the drive voltage less the 0.7 V of the base-emitter junction, at the base current you want.
cards.hint: Voltage across the resistor ÷ the current, in amps.

cards.title: PNP: switching the supply side
cards.body:
A **PNP** transistor is the mirror image. **Emitter to the supply**, the load from the **collector to 0 V**. Pull the base about **0.7 V below** the emitter (current flows **out** of the base) and it turns on.

It switches the supply side of the load: a **high-side** switch that **sources** current.

That is what a **PNP sensor** and a **sourcing PLC output** are: when on, they connect the load to +24 V. NPN sensors and **sinking** outputs connect it to 0 V. Match them to the input or load they drive.
cards.more:
Many machines prefer the load's bottom end at 0 V all the time, and the switching done at the top (PNP, sourcing), so that a wire chafing to the earthed frame cannot switch a load on. That is the usual UK and European choice for sensors and PLC I/O.

To turn a PNP on from a logic output, you have to pull its base down towards 0 V. If the supply is 24 V and the logic is 5 V, a 5 V output cannot turn it off (the base can never get up near 24 V), so a small NPN is often used to pull the PNP's base down: two transistors, one switch.

The arrow on the symbol points out of the emitter on an NPN (Not Pointing iN) and into it on a PNP.

cards.q: A PNP proximity sensor's output is on. What does its black wire connect to?
options: +24 V: it sources current to the load
0 V: it sinks current from the load
Nothing until the PLC polls it
Earth, through the sensor body
cards.why: PNP is a high-side switch: on, it connects its output to the supply, so current flows out of it, through the PLC input, to 0 V. An NPN sensor's output connects to 0 V instead.

cards.title: MOSFETs: switched by voltage
cards.body:
A **MOSFET** has a **gate**, a **drain** and a **source**. An N-channel MOSFET is the NPN's cousin: source to 0 V, load to the drain. A **voltage** on the gate (not a current) turns it on.

Fully on, it behaves like a small **resistance**, $R_{DS(on)}$, often a few milliohms to an ohm, so its heat is $P = I^2 R_{DS(on)}$.

What it needs:

- enough gate voltage: a **logic-level** MOSFET for a 3.3 or 5 V driver
- a small **gate resistor** (say 100 Ω) and a **pull-down** (say 10 kΩ) so it stays off when the driver is off
cards.more:
The gate is like the plate of a capacitor: once charged, it holds the MOSFET on with no current flowing in. That makes MOSFETs ideal where a microcontroller drives several amps.

The catch is the gate voltage. A standard MOSFET may need 10 V on its gate to be fully on; at 5 V it is half-on and gets hot. 'Logic-level' parts are rated fully on at 4.5 V (some at 2.5 V): check $R_{DS(on)}$ at your gate voltage on the datasheet.

The pull-down matters at power-up: while a microcontroller boots, its pins float, and a floating gate can turn the MOSFET half on.

Numbers: 2 A through 0.05 Ω: $2^2 \times 0.05 = 0.2$ W. A BJT carrying 2 A at 0.2 V would waste 0.4 W and need 40 mA or more of base current.

cards.q: A MOSFET with an on-resistance of {r} Ω carries {i} A. How much power does it turn into heat?
cards.why: Fully on, a MOSFET is a small resistor: $P = I^2 R$. Double the current, four times the heat.

cards.q: A 5 V microcontroller pin must switch a 24 V relay coil that draws 150 mA, using an NPN transistor with a minimum gain of 100. Design the base drive.

steps.show: $\frac{5 - 0.7}{0.0045} = 956$ Ω, so the standard 910 Ω (or 1 kΩ, at a slightly lower 4.3 mA)
A flyback diode across the coil, band to +24 V; the transistor's emitter and the microcontroller's 0 V joined.

cards.why: Load current to base current to resistor, then protect against the coil's switch-off spike. The two supplies must share 0 V, or the base current has nowhere to return.

cards.q: Why does step 2 give three times the minimum base current?
cards.model: The gain on the datasheet is a range, and it falls when the transistor is cold or carrying a lot of current. Driving only the bare minimum would leave some transistors half-on, with several volts across them at 150 mA, which wastes power and can overheat them. Three times the minimum makes sure any transistor of that type is fully saturated, at the cost of a few more milliamps from the pin.
points: Gain falls with temperature and current
Half-on means volts across it and heat

cards.q: A 24 V PLC output switches a 24 V lamp that draws 400 mA through an NPN with a minimum gain of 80. Choose the base resistor for an overdrive of 2.

steps.show: $P = I^2 R = 0.0106^2 \times 2200 = 0.25$ W: use a 0.5 W resistor

cards.why: From 24 V the base resistor drops a lot of voltage, so check its power too.

cards.q: A {vin} V output must saturate a transistor carrying {ic} mA, minimum gain {h}, overdrive 3. What base resistor?
cards.why: Base current from the load, gain and overdrive; then the resistor from the drive voltage.
cards.hint: Base current first, then the resistor.

cards.q: A saturated transistor has {vce} V across it while carrying {ic} mA. How much power does it waste, in mW?
cards.why: Power is voltage times current: V × mA gives mW. Saturated, it is small; half-on with 10 V across it, the same current would waste 50 times more.

cards.q: A transistor switching a relay coil fails after a few days. One line of the design is the cause. Which?
lines: Base resistor worked out for 4.5 mA
Relay coil 24 V, 150 mA, between +24 V and the collector
No diode across the coil, to save a part
Emitter to 0 V, joined to the logic's 0 V
cards.fix: Fit a flyback diode across the coil, band to +24 V
cards.why: At every switch-off the coil makes a spike of hundreds of volts on the collector, far past the transistor's rating, and it eventually fails. The diode gives the coil's current a path and clamps the spike.

cards.q: A switching transistor runs hot. With it on, a meter reads 6 V from collector to emitter. What is wrong?
options: Too little base drive: it is not saturated
Too much base drive: it is over-saturated
The load is drawing too little current
Nothing: 6 V is normal when on
cards.why: Saturated, a BJT has about 0.2 V across it. 6 V means it is only half on, wasting 6 V × the current as heat. Give it more base current (a smaller base resistor) or check the gain.

cards.q: A 3.3 V microcontroller drives a standard MOSFET's gate directly. The MOSFET gets hot at 3 A. Why?
options: 3.3 V does not turn a standard MOSFET fully on
MOSFETs need gate current, not voltage
3 A is always too much for any MOSFET
The pull-down resistor is too large
cards.why: A standard MOSFET may need about 10 V on its gate for its rated $R_{DS(on)}$. At 3.3 V it is only partly on, with a much higher resistance, so $I^2 R$ is large. Use a logic-level MOSFET rated at the gate voltage you have, or a gate driver.

cards.q: Match each device with how it switches.
pairs: Sinks: connects the load to 0 V
Sources: connects the load to +24 V
cards.why: NPN and sinking switch the 0 V side; PNP and sourcing switch the supply side. A PNP sensor needs a sinking input (one whose common is at 0 V).

cards.q: A 2 V LED is to run at 20 mA from a {vs} V supply, switched on its 0 V side by a saturated transistor dropping 0.2 V. What series resistor?
cards.why: The diodes lesson's rule, with one more drop in the path: the transistor's 0.2 V when saturated. Leaving it out makes only a small difference at 24 V, more at 5 V.
cards.hint: Supply less the LED and the transistor, over the current.

cards.q: You worked out a base resistor of 860 Ω. Which standard value do you fit?
options: 820 Ω: a little more base current
910 Ω: a little less base current
1 MΩ: much safer for the pin
8.6 Ω: the nearest round number
cards.why: Rounding down the resistor rounds the base current up, which keeps the transistor saturated. 910 Ω would still work with an overdrive built in, but erring towards more drive is the rule.

cards.q: A transistor carries {ic} mA. Half-on, it has {vce} V across it. How much does it waste, in W, compared with about 0.2 V when saturated?
cards.why: Same current, many times the voltage across it, so many times the heat. That is why a switch must be fully on.

cards.q: What turns a PNP high-side switch on?
options: Pulling its base about 0.7 V below its emitter
Raising its base well above its emitter
Connecting its collector to the supply
Removing all current from its base
cards.why: A PNP is the mirror of an NPN: current flows out of its base when the base is pulled below the emitter (which sits at the supply).

cards.q: {vin} V drive, {ib} mA base current wanted. Base resistor?
cards.why: Drive voltage less 0.7 V, over the base current in amps.

cards.q: About what voltage is across a saturated NPN switch?
options: About 0.2 V
About 0.7 V
Half the supply
The full supply
cards.why: Saturated, $V_{CE}$ is about 0.1–0.3 V. 0.7 V is the base-emitter drop; the full supply would mean it is off.
